evidence_quotes.quote: This research indicates the housing struggles of the urban poor and the emerging City-community engagement in urban services provision (water, sanitation, tenure security and roads) and changing municipal attitudes towards the urban poor.
The objective of this research is to investigate how the Harare slum upgrading programme is promoting inclusive municipal governance.

Key informant interviews were conducted with City of Harare and Dialogue on Shelter ofﬁcers and were premised on experiences with the project, changes over time and impacts in terms of inclusiveness of Harare City and opportunities that remain available to impact inclusive governance.

evidence_quotes.quote: The 2012 Dzivarasekwa Extension enumeration revealed that there were 121 plastic shacks, 76 grass-thatched shacks, 70 shallow unprotected wells, 18 deep protected wells, 1 borehole, and 88 pit latrines and insecure tenure (ZIHOPFE, City of Harare & Dialogue on Shelter, 2012). At present, slum dwellers are living in a planned settlement, with reticulated water and sewer and road infrastructure.
Slum upgrading in Harare utilises free resources such as land, gravel, water and labour from the city of Harare and labour contribution by the targeted slum dwellers.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household water and sanitation service access in Harare's Dzivarasekwa Extension as part of slum upgrading, documenting the shift from shallow wells and pit latrines/sky-loos to reticulated municipal water and sewer connections for 480 households, as well as post-connection water and sewer bill arrears.
criterion_notes.c2: Passes the plain wording of Criterion 2 (plain_criterion2_decision = include) because it examines inclusive municipal governance, gradual institutional change, municipal-NGO-CBO institutional partnerships, and participatory urban planning in Harare. Fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading (c2_legal_admin_factor = no): the study evaluates a Gates Foundation-funded slum-upgrading project and broad participatory municipal-community partnership primarily aimed at housing delivery, in which reticulated water and sewer pipes were installed as bundled physical project infrastructure. References to rigid town planning standards (as bottlenecks to low-cost housing, with City housing policy not yet revised), incremental housing development, Federation stand-allocation criteria, and two sentences on post-upgrade municipal bill arrears are descriptive housing-project features rather than an empirical analysis of a legal, regulatory, or administrative rule directly governing water or sanitation service access.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary qualitative empirical evidence from focus group discussions, key informant interviews (3 Dialogue on Shelter officers, 3 City of Harare officers, and 50 project beneficiaries), individual beneficiary case profiles, and settlement enumeration/project documents.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports household and settlement access outcomes in Dzivarasekwa Extension: transition from 70 shallow unprotected wells, 18 deep protected wells, 1 borehole, and 88 pit latrines to reticulated water and sewer infrastructure for 480 households (approximately 2,016 people), alongside affordability challenges with municipal water and sewer bills exceeding US$100 per household.
criterion_notes.c5: Identifies the population and units of analysis (urban poor / slum households in Dzivarasekwa Extension, Harare, and municipal/civil-society actors), exposure (the Harare Slum Upgrading Programme and municipal-community partnership), outcomes (housing/tenure titles and reticulated water and sewer access), and study design (qualitative empirical case study).

study_design: Qualitative empirical case study (focus group discussions, key informant interviews, individual beneficiary case profiles, and project/enumeration document analysis)
population_and_sample: Urban poor / slum dwellers in Harare, Zimbabwe (480 upgraded beneficiary households / est. 2,016 people in Dzivarasekwa Extension; 62 slums profiled city-wide with 37,936 households); qualitative sample of 50 project beneficiaries, 3 City of Harare officers, 3 Dialogue on Shelter officers, and Federation coordinators
exposure: Harare Slum Upgrading Programme (2010-2015 Gates Foundation-supported municipal-community partnership among City of Harare, Dialogue on Shelter, and Zimbabwe Homeless People's Federation involving participatory urban planning, slum profiling/enumeration, and incremental settlement upgrading)
outcome: Inclusive municipal governance, housing/land ownership (249 sectional and 231 individual titles), and household transition from shallow wells and pit latrines to reticulated water and sewer infrastructure for 480 households (plus post-upgrade municipal water and sewer bill arrears exceeding US$100 per household)
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure) per the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification. While the study empirically documents household transitions from shallow wells and pit latrines to reticulated water and sewer infrastructure in Harare's Dzivarasekwa Extension and would be included under the literal broad wording of Criterion 2 (plain_criterion2_decision = include), its exposure is a donor-funded slum-upgrading project and participatory municipal-community governance partnership focused on housing delivery rather than a rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism directly governing water or sanitation service access.
